1.question: Why did Jesus talk so much about money?
1.answer: Because He knew where it leads. As He said in Matthew 6:21, “Your heart will always be where your treasure is.” The money leads and the heart follows, so money doesn’t just reveal what we love; it trains what we love. That makes it one of the main places where discipleship happens, or doesn’t.

1.question: Does the Bible teach that God will make generous Christians rich?
1.answer: No. The book rejects the teaching that giving or believing enough binds God to repay in cash. God does bless generosity, but Jesus was poor, Paul knew hunger, and the heroes of Hebrews 11 went about “lacking everything.” As the introduction puts it, “Any gospel that would embarrass the apostles is not the gospel.”

1.question: Is money itself evil according to the Bible?
1.answer: No. Abraham, Job, Joseph of Arimathea and Lydia all had wealth, and the Bible never calls money evil. It says “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10). The problem is not in your wallet. It is in the heart that holds it.

2.question: What does the Bible say about who owns our money and possessions?
2.answer: Everything belongs to God. “The earth is the LORD’s, and all that fills it” (Psalm 24:1), and “The silver belongs to Me, and the gold belongs to Me” (Haggai 2:8). Even Israel’s land could never be sold for good, because it was His. We hold our homes, savings, income and skills, but we do not own them.

2.question: What does it mean for a Christian to be a steward of money?
2.answer: A steward is a manager who runs a household for the master, as Joseph did in Potiphar’s house, holding the keys to everything and owning none of it. So the question changes from “What do I want to do with my money?” to “What does the owner want done with His money?” The whole hundred percent is His, not only the part we give.

2.question: Why did Moses warn Israel that prosperity would make them forget God?
2.answer: In Deuteronomy 8:17-18 Moses saw that comfort brings a temptation hardship never had: to say, “My own power and the strength of my own hands have won me this wealth.” He told them to remember that God gives the ability to grow wealthy. Forgetting God is rarely dramatic; it is a slow drift that comes with having more.

3.question: Is work a curse according to the Bible?
3.answer: No. God gave Adam work in Eden before there was sin, “to work it and take care of it” (Genesis 2:15). The curse in Genesis 3 made work painful, but it did not make it bad. Work was God’s idea, God Himself is a worker, and Jesus spent most of His life in a carpenter’s shop.

3.question: What did Paul mean by “Anyone who will not work should not eat”?
3.answer: Paul was writing to believers in Thessalonica who could work but had stopped and were busy with everyone else’s business. It is not cruelty to those who cannot work, since the same Bible commands generous care for the sick, the old, the widow and the orphan. Earning your own bread is part of your dignity and keeps you from being a burden.

3.question: How can ordinary work be worship for a Christian?
3.answer: Paul told slaves, who had the hardest jobs in the Roman world, to work “as for the Lord and not for people” (Colossians 3:23-24). If that was true for them, it is true of the spreadsheet, the shift at the till or the night on the ward. There is no secular job for a Christian, only work done for Christ or for ourselves.

4.question: Why does the Bible call greed idolatry?
4.answer: Paul calls greed “idolatry” (Colossians 3:5) because an idol is anything we look to for what only God can give. Jesus speaks of mammon almost as a rival lord: money offers security, status, comfort, freedom and control, and asks to be trusted. It is the idol of choice for respectable people, because you can worship it without ever going near a shrine.

4.question: How can a Christian tell whether money has become their master?
4.answer: The chapter offers honest tests: where your mind goes when it is free, what makes you anxious, what you would refuse to give up if Jesus asked, what your bank statement says about what you value, and what gets cut first when times are tight. Martyn Lloyd-Jones noted that the first economy is often “our contribution to God’s work.”

4.question: How can a Christian break free from serving money?
4.answer: Not by simply trying harder, but by letting a better master take its place. Money is a hard master that always wants more and never says “Well done,” while Jesus says, “My yoke is easy to wear, and the load I give is light.” When we see how good He is, money’s promises start to look thin.

5.question: What does 2 Corinthians 8:9 mean when it says Jesus became poor to make us rich?
5.answer: Jesus shared the Father’s glory and made the stars, yet He emptied Himself, was born to poor parents, had nowhere to lay His head, and on the cross lost even the sense of His Father’s presence. The riches He gives are not money but forgiveness, adoption, the Holy Spirit and eternal life, “the riches of Christ.”

5.question: What is the deepest reason a Christian gives money?
5.answer: Not because we have to, but because of what Jesus did. Without that foundation, giving becomes a duty, a tax, a way to feel good, or an attempt to earn God’s favour, and it wears us out. When we see what Jesus gave for us, giving becomes a response, the natural overflow of a heart that has been made rich.

5.question: Should Christians feel ashamed of past failures with money?
5.answer: The good news is not “Try harder with your money” but that Jesus became poor to make you rich. Your failures with money are among the sins He carried, and your worth to God does not rise or fall with your bank balance or giving record. Receive His riches first, then learn to handle the smaller riches He has given you.

6.question: What does the tenth commandment mean by coveting?
6.answer: To covet is to want something that isn’t yours so much that it takes hold of you: a restless “if only” that looks at another’s house, job or life and says, “I deserve that more than they do.” Achan’s confession shows its path: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid. It starts not with the taking, but with the wanting.

6.question: How did Thomas Watson define covetousness?
6.answer: Borrowing from Augustine, Watson called covetousness Plus velle quam sat est, “to desire more than enough.” It is not about having a lot or a little but about never being able to say “enough,” so a poor person can be eaten up with it and a rich person free of it. It is a condition of the heart, not of the bank account.

6.question: How can a Christian fight covetousness?
6.answer: A heart cannot simply be emptied; it must be filled with something better. The chapter names four weapons: gratitude, which notices what we already have; generosity, which loosens money’s grip; guarding your eyes, since Achan’s sin began with “I saw”; and treasuring God, because covetousness is at root a worship problem.

7.question: What did Paul mean when he said he had learned the secret of contentment?
7.answer: Writing from prison, Paul said he had “learned to be content” and been “let into the secret” of living with little or with plenty (Philippians 4:11-13). Contentment was not his personality but a skill learned in a hard school: a settled peace in God that says, whatever the bank balance, “I have enough, because I have God.”

7.question: Is Philippians 4:13 about achieving success?
7.answer: No. People quote “I have strength for every situation in the one who makes me strong” as if it were about winning a race or passing an exam. In context it is about being content when you are hungry. Christ gives the strength to be at peace with little and the strength to stay humble with much.

7.question: What is Christian contentment not?
7.answer: It is not laziness, since Paul made tents through the night; not pretending, since he named his hunger plainly; and not settling for injustice, since Christians should work to change unfair systems. Nor is it only for hard times, because plenty brings its own temptations of pride, self-reliance and forgetting God.

8.question: Why did God tell Israel not to keep manna overnight?
8.answer: God was teaching His people to depend on Him one day at a time. Those who kept extra found it crawling with worms by morning, yet whoever gathered much or little always had enough (Exodus 16:17-18). Jesus taught the same daily trust when He told us to pray, “Give us today the bread we need.”

8.question: What does Jesus mean by “seek the kingdom” first in Matthew 6:33?
8.answer: It is not a bargain that makes God owe us whatever we want. It is a matter of priorities: God’s rule, purposes and righteousness get our first attention, best energy and first money. When God is first, everything else falls into place and our Father takes responsibility for our needs, though He has promised needs, not wants.

8.question: How can a Christian move from worrying about money to trusting God?
8.answer: Not all at once but, like the manna, one day at a time. The chapter suggests turning worries into prayers, remembering God’s record of provision, living in today since “tomorrow can take care of its own worries,” and doing the next right thing, such as applying for the job or talking to the bank, then resting.

9.question: Why did Jesus tell the rich young man to sell everything?
9.answer: The young man was sincere and had kept the commandments, and Jesus “looked at him and loved him.” But his wealth was the idol keeping him from Jesus, and he went away sad, “for he owned a great deal of property.” Jesus doesn’t ask this of everyone: Zacchaeus gave half, and Joseph of Arimathea kept his tomb.

9.question: Why does the Bible say riches are dangerous?
9.answer: The chapter gives five reasons: riches compete for our trust in God, their “false promises” choke the word like thorns, they make us proud, they blind us as they blinded the church in Laodicea, and they make us forget others, like the rich man who never saw Lazarus at his gate.

9.question: What does Paul tell rich Christians to do in 1 Timothy 6:17-19?
9.answer: Not to be proud, not to put their hope in uncertain wealth but in God, to enjoy His gifts with thanks, and to give generously and share. Giving is the key: it is how a rich person keeps riches from becoming a master, and it stores up treasure so they “may take hold of the life that is truly life.”

10.question: What did John Wesley mean by “Gain all you can”?
10.answer: In his sermon “The Use of Money,” Wesley urged Christians to work hard and earn well, saying the fault “does not lie in the money, but in them that use it.” But he set conditions: gain without hurting your body, your mind or soul, or your neighbour. Gaining is only the first rule, the starting point for saving and giving.

10.question: What are the marks of honest work for a Christian?
10.answer: Do a full day’s work with an undivided heart, charge a fair price, pay those you employ promptly and fairly, pay your taxes, choose work that harms no one’s body or soul, and be content with your pay without grabbing what isn’t yours. Zacchaeus, who promised to repay four times what he had cheated, shows how seriously this is meant.

10.question: Why is honesty in business a Christian witness?
10.answer: People may never read your Bible, but they will read your invoices. A plumber who refuses to overcharge or an employee who owns up to a costly mistake shows the world what God is like, while Christians who cheat damage the reputation of Jesus. “Better a little gained honestly than a fortune made by injustice” (Proverbs 16:8).

11.question: What does Jesus’ parable of the unfinished tower teach about money?
11.answer: In Luke 14:28 the builder who doesn’t first add up the expense lays a foundation, runs out of money and becomes a joke. Jesus told it about the cost of discipleship, but used an everyday picture because the principle is so obviously true: wise people plan before they spend. “The plans of the diligent bring nothing but gain” (Proverbs 21:5).

11.question: What are the basic parts of a Christian budget?
11.answer: A budget is deciding ahead of time where God’s money will go, instead of finding out afterwards where it went. At its simplest it has four parts: what comes in after tax, what goes to God first, what you need to live, and what’s left for saving and then other spending. Most people find a plan brings freedom.

11.question: What did John Wesley mean by “Save all you can”?
11.answer: Wesley mainly meant don’t waste money: don’t spend it on things that only feed pride, vanity or the desire to be seen, and live simply so that more is left over. It was a guard against waste so there would be more to give, not a commendation of hoarding, freeing money for his third rule, “Give all you can.”

12.question: Does the Bible say all debt is sin?
12.answer: No. The law gave rules for lending, Jesus said not to turn away someone who wants to borrow, and a carefully planned mortgage can be wise. But the Bible treats debt as something to avoid where possible and leave as soon as you can: “Do not stay in debt to anyone, except for the debt of love” (Romans 13:8). And what we borrow must be repaid.

12.question: What does the story of Elisha and the widow’s oil teach about debt?
12.answer: The widow’s husband had died in debt, and the creditor was coming to take her two sons as slaves. God filled every borrowed jar with oil so she could sell it, pay the debt and live on the rest (2 Kings 4:7). It is a story of God’s provision, and also of how terrible debt can be.

12.question: How can a Christian get out of debt?
12.answer: Stop digging by taking on no new debt; face the facts by listing every debt, rate and payment; make a plan; get help, since pride keeps more people in debt than poverty does; keep giving, even a little; pray, as the widow in Elisha’s day did; and be patient, celebrating every debt you pay off.

13.question: What does the Bible say about providing for your family?
13.answer: “Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). Written mainly about elderly widows in a world without pensions, it applies to spouse, children and ageing parents. Providing for them is not a distraction from serving God; it is part of it.

13.question: What did William Seymour teach about money in “In Money Matters”?
13.answer: Seymour, of the Azusa Street revival, warned against teachers who told new believers to sell everything, leaving children half naked and spouses abandoned. He warned just as strongly against having property and money banked up while others suffer. “It is right for you to have property,” he wrote, but if the Lord says to give, “you do it.”

13.question: Is buying insurance or making a will a lack of faith?
13.answer: No. Joseph stored grain for the famine and nobody accuses him of unbelief; wise provision is a form of love. Providing covers daily needs, an emergency fund, protection such as insurance, saving for old age and making a will, and also time and presence, because children need a parent more than a bigger house.

14.question: Why does the Bible say to give God the first of our income?
14.answer: Proverbs 3:9-10 asks for “the first and best,” not the leftovers. Giving first is an act of faith that trusts God for the rest, an act of worship that puts “seek the kingdom” first into practice, and plain wisdom, because spending expands to fill whatever is available and the end of the month usually finds nothing left.

14.question: Is the tithe the limit of Christian giving?
14.answer: The chapter calls the tithe “a wonderful starting line but not a ceiling.” Faithful Christians disagree on whether it is still required, but if Israel gave a tenth under the old covenant, those who have received so much more in Christ should hardly give less. The Macedonians, Zacchaeus and the widow all went beyond it.

14.question: Does Malachi 3:10 promise that God will repay givers with money?
14.answer: The promises are real and God does bless generosity, but His blessing is not always financial; Jesus, the most generous person who ever lived, died owning only His clothes. Give because you love and trust God, not as an investment scheme. He will make sure you never lose by being generous, but He decides how He repays, in this life or the next.

15.question: What does it mean that “God loves a cheerful giver”?
15.answer: God isn’t short of funds; He wants our hearts, and gladness shows the heart is in it. You won’t always feel happy when you give, and sometimes the joy comes later, but giving should never be squeezed out by guilt, pressure or manipulation, “not with regret and not because you feel you must.” Gratitude for Christ’s gift is the soil it grows in.

15.question: Why did George Müller warn against giving only on impulse?
15.answer: Müller said that whoever neglects habitual, regular giving “from principle and upon scriptural ground” and leaves it “only to feeling and impulse” will “certainly be a loser.” Paul likewise asked the Corinthians to settle their gift in their hearts and set money aside weekly. Planned giving also leaves you free to meet special needs.

15.question: Does Jesus forbid all public giving?
15.answer: No. In Matthew 6:1-4 Jesus warns that those who give for show “have already been paid in full,” while the Father who sees what is hidden will repay. Yet the early church knew Barnabas sold a field and gave the money, and an example can inspire others. The question is motive: am I giving to be seen by people, or by God?

16.question: What does the Bible say about God’s care for the poor?
16.answer: From one end of the Bible to the other, God defends the poor, the widow, the orphan and the foreigner. The law left field edges for gleaners, sent the third-year tithe to the needy and cancelled debts every seventh year, and Moses said, “open your hand to him generously.” Oppressing the poor insults the One who made them (Proverbs 14:31).

16.question: What did Jesus mean when He said that serving the least was done for Him?
16.answer: In Matthew 25 the King tells the righteous that when He was hungry, thirsty, a stranger, without clothes, sick or in prison, they cared for Him. “Each time you did it for one of these My brothers and sisters, even the least of them, you did it for Me.” Jesus identified Himself with the poor completely: when you feed a hungry person, you feed Him.

16.question: What happened when John Wesley spent his money on pictures?
16.answer: At Oxford on a cold winter’s day, a young maid called at his room wearing only a thin linen gown. Reaching to give her something, he found he had almost nothing left, having just bought pictures for his walls. He rebuked himself: “Thou hast adorned thy walls with the money which might have screened this poor creature from the cold!”

17.question: How does God measure the size of a gift?
17.answer: Not by its size but by its cost. The rich gave from their surplus, but the widow, with two tiny coins, gave “the whole of what she had to live on” (Mark 12:43-44). A small sacrificial gift may be worth more in heaven than a large gift given from comfort, as Charles Finney told the wealthy church members of his day.

17.question: How did John Wesley live out his rule “Give all you can”?
17.answer: As a young man at Oxford, Wesley found he could live on about twenty-eight pounds a year and gave the rest away. When his income doubled and rose further, he kept living on the same amount and gave everything else. Late in life his books earned a great deal, and almost all of it went to the poor and the gospel.

17.question: What is lifestyle creep, and how can Christians resist it?
17.answer: Lifestyle creep is letting spending rise to match every pay rise, with a bigger house, a newer car and dearer holidays, until we feel as stretched as before. Setting a ceiling on spending, deciding what we need to live on “simply but not miserably,” lets giving grow instead. It is a way of saying “Enough,” the opposite of covetousness.

18.question: What happened when Hudson Taylor gave away his last half-crown?
18.answer: Called to a starving family in Hull, Taylor realised he could trust God “plus one-and-sixpence” but not with nothing, and his conscience asked how he dared call God Father with that coin in his pocket. He gave it, and joy flooded back. The next morning a letter brought a pair of gloves and half a sovereign, four times what he had given.

18.question: What does Jesus teach in Luke 16:10 about being faithful with money?
18.answer: How we handle money, a small and passing thing, reveals and shapes our character for large things. That is sobering, because there is no such thing as a small compromise. It is also encouraging, because you don’t have to be rich to be faithful: a widow with two coins and a millionaire with a fortune face the same test.

18.question: Why was the third servant in the parable of the talents condemned?
18.answer: Given one bag of silver, he buried it, saying he was afraid of his master, who called him wicked and lazy. The lesson is that God gives different people different amounts and expects each to be faithful and put it to work for Him. The great sin in the parable is not losing money but doing nothing with it out of fear.

19.question: How was the ministry of Jesus funded?
19.answer: Luke tells us that as Jesus travelled from town to town, women including Mary Magdalene and Joanna, the wife of Herod’s household manager, “were using their own resources to provide for them” (Luke 8:3). From the beginning, the spread of the gospel depended on God’s people opening their homes and their purses.

19.question: What did Paul mean by the “profit” in the Philippians’ account?
19.answer: Paul told the Philippians, his partners in the gospel, that he was not after the gift but “the profit that keeps adding up in your account” (Philippians 4:17). Those who give to support the gospel share in the fruit of the work. The famous promise that God “will fill every need you have” was written to these generous givers, not to hoarders.

19.question: What did E. M. Bounds say about money and prayer in mission?
19.answer: Bounds warned that “money without prayer is powerless in the face of the darkness, the wretchedness and the sin” of unreached lands, and noticed that “our contributions of money exceed our offerings of prayer.” The mission is advanced by the Holy Spirit through prayer; money serves that work but is never a substitute for it.

20.question: What does the Bible say about teaching children about money?
20.answer: Deuteronomy 6:6-7 places teaching in the ordinary rhythms of home: sitting in the house, walking on the road, lying down and rising. Children learn about money in the supermarket, in the car and when the bills come in. But the words must first be on the parent’s own heart, because you can’t pass on what you don’t have.

20.question: What money lessons should Christian parents teach their children?
20.answer: That God owns everything, that work is good, to give first (many families use Give, Save and Spend jars), to save for something, to spend wisely by making small mistakes, to be content despite the adverts, that debt is dangerous, and to care for the poor. Above all, children learn more from what we do than from what we say.

20.question: What did John Wesley advise parents to teach their children about riches?
20.answer: Wesley urged parents to instil early “a fear and contempt of pomp and grandeur; an abhorrence and dread of the love of money” and a deep conviction “that riches cannot give happiness.” He wanted children to fear not money but the love of money, and to despise not work but showing off.

21.question: What does the Bible say about giving an account of our money to God?
21.answer: “All of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). For a Christian this is not a judgment about salvation, which was settled at the cross, but about our faithfulness with what God entrusted to us, including money. Wesley’s sermon “The Good Steward” taught that all of it was lent to us.

21.question: What does it mean to store up treasure in heaven?
21.answer: What we give away for Christ and His kingdom is not lost but sent ahead, stored where moths, rust and thieves can’t touch it. As C. T. Studd wrote, “Only one life, ’twill soon be past, only what’s done for Christ will last.” We are not saved by giving, but God rewards His children’s faithfulness far beyond what they deserve.

21.question: Is there hope for a Christian who has been a poor steward of money?
21.answer: Yes. Every one of us has failed with money in some way, and God’s grace is bigger than our failures; the thief on the cross had nothing to give, yet Jesus welcomed him into paradise. Start where you are, repent, receive His forgiveness and begin to be faithful today. It is never too late to lay up treasure in heaven.

22.question: What is a Christian rule of life for money?
22.answer: A rule of life is a simple set of written commitments that shape how a Christian lives. It is not a set of laws to earn God’s favour, but “more like a trellis that helps a plant grow in the right direction.” The book’s suggested rule builds on Wesley’s three rules and invites readers to adapt it and write their own.

22.question: What are the ten commitments in the rule of life for money?
22.answer: Remember that it all belongs to God; gain all I can, honestly; give first; save all I can; stay free of unnecessary debt; provide for my own; give all I can, with a limit on my lifestyle; guard my heart; pass it on to the next generation; and live with the end in view, seeking to hear “Well done.”

22.question: What does the parable of the treasure hidden in a field teach about money?
22.answer: The man who found the treasure sold everything with joy, not feeling it a sacrifice, because he knew he had found something worth more than everything else. Christ is that treasure. When you have found Him, you can hold money loosely, give it freely, manage it faithfully and enjoy it gratefully, because your heart is already full.

23.question: How does the 30-day reading plan on money work?
23.answer: It takes the book’s thirty key verses, one for each day of a month. Read the verse slowly, then a little of the chapter around it in your Bible, and ask two questions: What does this show me about God? What does it ask of me? Each day ends with a short prayer.

23.question: How is the 30-day reading plan organised?
23.answer: It follows the book’s five parts: Week 1, Whose is it?; Week 2, the heart behind the wallet; Week 3, wisdom for everyday money; Week 4, generous like God; and Days 28 to 30, treasure that lasts. Each day pairs a key verse with a short reflection question or prompt, such as “Where is my treasure? Where is my heart?”

23.question: Which verses begin and end the 30-day reading plan on money?
23.answer: Day 1 is Psalm 24:1, “The earth is the LORD’s,” asking what I treat as mine that is really His. Day 30 is Matthew 25:21, “Well done, good and faithful servant,” inviting you to pray that you will hear these words one day and to write down one commitment you want to keep.

24.question: What are the steps of the one-page money plan?
24.answer: There are eight: write what comes in after tax; decide what goes to God first; list what you need to live; decide your saving; plan your freedom from debt; set amounts for everything else; check the balance; and review at the end of the month. A sheet of paper, a pencil and an honest hour are enough, done together if you are married.

24.question: How do you check that a monthly money plan balances?
24.answer: Add up Steps 2 to 6: giving, essentials, saving, debt and everything else. The total should equal your income in Step 1. If it is more, you are spending more than you earn, so go back and cut until it balances; if it is less, decide where the extra goes, perhaps to giving, saving or paying off debt faster.

24.question: How should savings and debts be handled in the one-page money plan?
24.answer: Start with a small emergency fund, then build toward three to six months of essential costs, then save for needs such as a home, old age or your children. List debts beyond the mortgage from smallest to largest with their interest rates, and decide how much extra to pay and which to clear first. Expect three or four months to get a plan that works.

25.question: How is the ten-week group guide organised?
25.answer: A group meets weekly for ten weeks, reading two chapters before each meeting, with the last week covering the final chapters and the Conclusion. Each meeting opens with prayer and a check-in on last week’s practice, reads each chapter’s key verse aloud, discusses chosen “For groups” questions, and commits to a new practice while praying for one another by name.

25.question: How can a small group talk about money safely?
25.answer: The guide sets three ground rules. Keep it safe: what is shared stays in the group, and nobody is pressured to share figures such as income or giving. Keep it honest: leaders go first with their own struggles. Keep it gracious: make room for those in debt and those quietly uncomfortable with wealth, aiming for grace and growth, not guilt.

25.question: Do you need to be a financial expert to lead a group study on money?
25.answer: No. A leader only needs to be honest, to love the people in the group, and to point them to Jesus. If someone shares a serious money problem such as heavy debt, help them find good advice and keep praying for them after the group ends. Above all, keep coming back to grace.
